MUQATIL:16:68-70/r4.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:16:68-70/r4.speaker: author
MUQATIL:16:68-70/r4.claim: God created people from nothing and takes them at their appointed times; some reach extreme old age and forget what they once knew, yet God knows resurrection will happen and is able to bring it about.

YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p74/r2.author: Yaḥyā b. Sallām
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p74/r2.speaker: author
YAHYA-SALLAM:v1p74/r2.claim: God creates people and then causes them to die; some reach extreme old age and become as unable to understand as a child.

FARRA:v2p109/r7.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v2p109/r7.speaker: author
FARRA:v2p109/r7.claim: لكيلا يعلم means that a person no longer understands anything after his earlier understanding.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p246#2/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p246#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p246#2/r1.claim: Ardhal al-ʿumur is old age, the worst and most diminished stage of life.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p246#2/r2.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p246#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p246#2/r2.claim: The person no longer knows what he once knew because old age has become severe.

TAB-FULL:v14p292#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p292#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p292#2/r1.claim: Al-Tabari says extreme old age can erase learned knowledge and reason, returning people to childhood ignorance; God, by contrast, never forgets or changes in knowledge and knows all past and future.

TAB-FULL:v14p292/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p292/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p292/r1.claim: God created people and takes their lives; some are returned to the worst stage of old age, with رذل describing a person who has become decrepit.

TAB-FULL:v14p292/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p292/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v14p292/r2.claim: Some say the worst age begins at seventy-five years.

TAB-FULL:v14p292/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v14p292/r3.speaker: علي
TAB-FULL:v14p292/r3.claim: Ali identifies seventy-five years as the age meant by the return to the worst stage of life.

ZAJJAJ:v3p211/r1.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p211/r1.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p211/r1.claim: Some age until senility takes their reason, becoming ignorant after knowledge; this displays God's power to reverse knowledge into ignorance.

ZAJJAJ:v3p211/r2.author: al-Zajjāj
ZAJJAJ:v3p211/r2.speaker: author
ZAJJAJ:v3p211/r2.claim: Life and death belong to God, and even the best food cannot extend a person's allotted lifespan.

NAHHAS:v2p402/r5.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p402/r5.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p402/r5.claim: The ‘most decrepit age’ is old age, when strength and intellect weaken; children may be weak too, but growth is expected for them.

NAHHAS:v2p402/r6.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v2p402/r6.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v2p402/r6.claim: In ‘so that he knows nothing,’ kāy governs the subjunctive and lā is an extra particle, so it does not block the verb.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r1.claim: أرذل العمر may mean the lowest and weakest stage of life, as the majority say.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r2.speaker: الكلبي
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r2.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies the worst age as old age.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r3.speaker: قطرب
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r3.claim: Qutrub identifies the worst age as eighty years.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r4.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r4.claim: Ali ibn Abi Talib identifies the worst age as seventy-five years.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r5.claim: The person returning to old age becomes ignorant again, as in childhood, or forgets former knowledge and cannot acquire new knowledge.

MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v3p200/r6.claim: A further possibility is that the verse means he no longer acts after knowing, using knowledge for action because old age impairs action more than knowledge.

QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r1.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r1.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r1.claim: Good provision may mean lawful food, unexpected sustenance, provision with no human obligation attached, or earnings acquired without disobedience or forgetfulness of God.

QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r5.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r5.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r5.claim: Humans are created with excellent outward and inward form, intelligence, reflection, knowledge, and judgment, yet old age brings decline and new pain.

QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r6.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r6.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r6.claim: One spiritual reading of the worst old age is falling from guidance into abandonment and sin after earlier obedience.

QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r7.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r7.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r7.claim: Another reading calls it a young seeker’s lapse after pursuing God for a time, when he breaks his resolve and returns to worldly aims; the path regards this as apostasy.

QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r8.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r8.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v2p162/r8.claim: Other readings identify the worst old age with an old man’s worldly craving, love of leadership, or accumulated injustices and unreconciled disputes.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r1.speaker: المفسرون
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r1.claim: The opening means God created people when they were nothing, then takes them at the end of their lifespans.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r10.speaker: عاصم عن عكرمة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r10.claim: He says a person who recites the Quran will not reach an age where he knows nothing after knowledge; the exception for believers and righteous deeds is explained as Quran reciters.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r2.claim: Ardhal al-ʿumur is the worst and lowest age; related forms describe the lowly followers in Hud and al-Shuʿaraʾ, and a parallel appears in al-Tin.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r3.speaker: السدي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r3.claim: Al-Suddi, transmitted by Asbat, glosses the lowest age as senility.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r4.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r4.claim: He identifies the lowest age as old age.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r5.speaker: قتادة
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r5.claim: He specifies ninety years as the lowest age.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r6.speaker: علي
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r6.claim: A report from Ali specifies seventy-five years as the lowest age.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r7.claim: The person returns to a childlike condition, forgetting what he learned because of age; Ibn Abbas likens him to a child without reason.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r8.speaker: أبو إسحاق
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r8.claim: He says the change from knowledge to ignorance demonstrates God's power just as death and life do.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r9.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p127#2/r9.claim: He says this does not happen to Muslims: longer life increases their honor, intelligence, and knowledge with God; he connects this with the exception for believers in al-Tin.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p130/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p130/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-BASIT:v13p130/r1.claim: God is knowing of what He has done to His allies and enemies, and powerful to do whatever He wills.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r2.claim: God creates people, takes them at their appointed times, and lets some reach decrepit old age, when they know nothing after once knowing things, like children without reason.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r3.claim: The source says this loss of knowledge does not happen to believers, because a believer's knowledge is not removed with age.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:16:69-70/r4.claim: God knows what people do and has power over what he wills.

JISHUMI:v6p4071/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v6p4071/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v6p4071/r6.claim: Arḏal means base or inferior; juhūd is denial while knowing the truth, as in the account of those who recognized the signs inwardly.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r1.claim: People die at different stages: as children, young people, or mature adults; the most decrepit age is the worst stage.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r2.speaker: مقاتل
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r2.claim: He identifies the most decrepit age with senility.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r3.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r3.claim: He says the most decrepit age begins at ninety.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r4.speaker: علي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r4.claim: A report from Ali puts the age at seventy-five; another view says eighty.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r5.claim: The person no longer understands anything after having understood things before.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r6.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAGHAWI-FULL:v5p30#2/r6.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet sought refuge from miserliness, laziness, decrepit age, the grave's punishment, the Dajjāl's trial, and life's and death's trials.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r1.claim: The verse recalls human creation from nonexistence and death, then points to people whose decline makes them an example of divine power.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r2.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r2.claim: Old age is the final stage, when senses fail and speech falters; it is called the lowest age despite infancy sharing such dependence, because infancy begins life with strong hope.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r3.speaker: علي رضي الله عنه
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r3.claim: A view transmitted from Ali places the beginning of the lowest age at seventy-five, a common pattern rather than a fixed limit.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r4.claim: There is no fixed age for this decline: one person may be decrepit at fifty while another at ninety is not.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r5.claim: The purpose-like lam describes an outcome: a person's knowledge dwindles after once knowing things, without implying that all knowledge literally disappears.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p407/r6.claim: God's knowledge and power do not change under events or time.

TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r4.speaker: سيبويه
TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r4.claim: For ‘so that after knowledge he knows nothing,’ Sibawayh makes ‘nothing’ the object of ʿalima and leaves the object of yaʿlamu implicit by way of explanation.

TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r5.speaker: الفراء
TABRISI:16:66-70#2/r5.claim: Al-Farrāʾ instead makes yaʿlamu operative, omits an object for ʿalima, and separates the object from its governing verb, combining two figurative constructions.

TABRISI:16:69-70/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:69-70/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:69-70/r10.claim: God created people, bestowed worldly and religious blessings, and then takes their lives.

TABRISI:16:69-70/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:69-70/r11.speaker: علي ع
TABRISI:16:69-70/r11.claim: A report from ʿAlī gives seventy-five years as the age of extreme old age; a similar report is attributed to the Prophet.

TABRISI:16:69-70/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:69-70/r12.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TABRISI:16:69-70/r12.claim: A report from ʿAlī gives seventy-five years as the age of extreme old age; a similar report is attributed to the Prophet.

TABRISI:16:69-70/r13.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:69-70/r13.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:16:69-70/r13.claim: Qatāda puts the age of extreme old age at ninety years.

TABRISI:16:69-70/r14.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:69-70/r14.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:69-70/r14.claim: At extreme old age people return toward childhood, forgetting what they once knew; alternatively, their knowledge simply diminishes compared with youth.

TABRISI:16:69-70/r15.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:16:69-70/r15.speaker: author
TABRISI:16:69-70/r15.claim: God knows what benefits His servants and has power over whatever He wills in managing and determining their circumstances.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r1.claim: God created people from nothing and takes their souls when their appointed lifespans end.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r2.speaker: علي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r2.claim: Ali defines the worst age as seventy-five years.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r5.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r5.claim: Al-Farra says old people may lose their earlier ability to reason.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r6.speaker: ابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r6.claim: Ibn Qutayba says severe old age can leave someone unable to know anything after once knowing about the world.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r7.speaker: الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r7.claim: Al-Zajjaj says some grow senile and become ignorant after being learned, demonstrating God's power to move people from knowledge to ignorance.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r8.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r8.claim: Ibn Abbas says this does not describe Muslims, who gain honor, reason, and knowledge with long life.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r9.speaker: عكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p467#2/r9.claim: Ikrima says whoever recites the Qur'an is not returned to the worst age.

RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r1.claim: After signs in animals, God points to human life stages: growth, youthful plateau, slight decline in middle age, and major decline in old age; the transitions show God acts as the mover, not nature.

RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r2.speaker: الطبائعيون
RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r2.claim: Naturalist physicians say the body begins from semen and menstrual blood, both hot and moist; heat consumes their moisture and hardens the developing organs and tissues.

RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r3.speaker: الطبائعيون
RAZI-FULL:v20p60#2/r3.claim: They say early life has excess moisture that permits growth until about 30 or 35; youth follows when moisture only suffices to preserve innate heat, lasting until about forty.

RAZI-FULL:v20p61#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p61#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p61#2/r1.claim: Naturalists say heat dries innate moisture, the loss of moisture weakens heat, and the two decline until death; Razi objects that nutrition could replace moisture and that their account circles through mutually dependent causes.

RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r1.speaker: الطبائعيون
RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r1.claim: Naturalists say decline begins when moisture no longer suffices to preserve innate heat: middle age is a subtle decline to sixty, old age an obvious decline to 120.

RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r2.claim: Razi argues prenatal heat transformed much more moisture into organs than it does after maturity; if heat alone caused development, it should dissipate moisture even faster in the mature body, contrary to observation.

RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p61/r3.claim: Innate heat in an adult cannot be merely the small amount present in semen, yet if it grows with the body, strength and health should rise forever; aging therefore is not explained by nature alone.

RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r1.claim: Razi concludes naturalists' account entails circular reasoning and is false; the stages of aging instead come from the all-powerful, wise, merciful creator, as illustrated by Q 77:20-24.

RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r2.claim: The rational argument confirms that God creates humans, causes death, and causes the shift from youth and health to old age, weakness, and loss of knowledge; these are not effects of nature.

RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r3.claim: God's knowledge and power explain these changes: nature cannot distinguish benefit from harm, whereas the world's creator knows benefits and can secure them and avert harms.

RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r4.claim: Arḏal al-ʿumur means the most wretched and weakest stage of life; the wording is linked to Q 26:111.

RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r5.speaker: المفسرون
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r5.claim: The commentators say God created people from nothing and takes them at the ends of their appointed lives.

RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p62/r6.claim: Razi raises two views on whether the verse's return to the most decrepit age includes Muslims or is restricted to disbelievers, but this excerpt does not give the views.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r1.speaker: علي
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r1.claim: ʿAlī identifies the “most decrepit age” as seventy-five years.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r2.speaker: قتادة
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r2.claim: Qatāda gives ninety years as the age meant by the phrase.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r3.speaker: السدي
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r3.claim: Al-Suddī interprets the phrase as senility.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r4.claim: Rāzī prefers long age: senility is loss of reason, which the verse presents as the end caused by reaching decrepit age; equating them makes cause and end identical.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r5.claim: A second view excludes Muslims, since long life only increases their honor with God; Rāzī supports it with the exception for believers in the cited verse.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r6.speaker: عكرمة
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r6.claim: ʿIkrima says a person who recites the Qurʾān will not be returned to decrepit age.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r7.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains “God is knowing” as knowledge of what He does to His allies and enemies.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r8.claim: The verse establishes both a freely acting Creator and resurrection: God first brought humans from nothing and can restore them after death.

RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v20p63/r9.claim: The alternation of life and death, and of childhood ignorance, adult knowledge, and old-age loss of reason, makes a second return to life and intellect possible.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r1.claim: Ardhal al-ʿumur means the worst and lowest age, when strength and intellect decline into senility and the like.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls it the lowest stage of life, when a person becomes like a child without reason.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r3.speaker: أنس بن مالك
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r3.claim: Al-Bukhārī reports from Anas that the Prophet sought refuge from laziness, cowardice, senility, and miserliness; a report from Saʿd adds seeking refuge from being returned to the lowest age.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r4.claim: Not knowing after knowledge means returning through extreme old age to childhood and forgetting matters once known.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r5.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r5.claim: One view says this loss of knowledge does not happen to a believer because a believer's knowledge is not taken away.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r6.speaker: قيل
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r6.claim: Another reading of the meaning is that the person no longer acts after knowing; action is expressed as knowledge because it depends on knowledge, and age affects action more.

QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:16:70/r7.claim: The argument addresses deniers of resurrection: the One who returns a person to this condition can cause death and then bring him back to life.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r1.claim: God takes people at differing appointed times; the most decrepit age is senility, when strength and reason decline as in childhood.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r2.speaker: قيل
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r2.claim: Some identify the decrepit age as ninety-five years; others say seventy-five.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r3.claim: Old age returns a person to childhood-like forgetfulness and poor understanding; God's knowledge encompasses lifespan and His power can take the vigorous young while leaving the frail old.

BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:16:70/r4.claim: The wide differences in lifespans show they result from a wise, powerful determiner rather than natural dispositions alone.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r1.claim: God takes people's souls; the most decrepit age is variously set at seventy-five, eighty, or ninety.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r2.claim: The purpose of extreme old age may be that a person forgets what was learned, or ceases to acquire further knowledge.

NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v2p263/r3.claim: God knows the wisdom of transforming people from their prime toward decline or from life toward extinction, and can change whatever He wills.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p561#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p561#2/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p561#2/r4.claim: After signs in livestock, fruits, and bees, the passage turns to God's complete power in creating humans from nothing, causing death, and changing them from ignorance to knowledge; hence عليم قدير closes the verse.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p561#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p561#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p561#2/r5.claim: The most decrepit age is the late period when senses, speech, and thought fail; it is called low because recovery is no longer expected, unlike childhood, which develops toward strength.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r1.speaker: علي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r1.claim: ʿAlī is reported to set the decrepit age at seventy-five, while Qatāda says ninety; the author says it differs by person, since some reach decrepitude at fifty and some centenarians do not.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r2.claim: The verse generally concerns anyone afflicted by senility and old age; another view limits it to unbelievers, citing the exception for believers who do good, while Qatāda says Qur'an reciters are not returned to decrepit age.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r3.claim: Al-Ḥawfī calls لام كي a reinforcing lam before كي, but the author follows grammatical analysts: the lam is causal and prepositional while كي is a verbal noun particle, with distinct functions.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r4.speaker: ابن عطية
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya takes the لام as indicating an eventual result: the aged person's state comes to resemble forgetfulness, a decline in knowledge rather than absolute ignorance; al-Zamakhsharī describes rapid forgetting after prior knowledge.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r5.claim: Other explanations say the person no longer grasps anything after prior understanding or gains no further knowledge; شيئا is governed either by the verbal noun or by يعلم, depending on the grammatical school.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p562/r6.claim: The verse contrasts human decline in power and knowledge with God's unchanging knowledge and power, matching the close عليم قدير.

SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r1.claim: In لكيلا, لام may mark purpose and كي is a source particle governing the subjunctive, with the phrase attached to يرد.

SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r2.speaker: الحوفي
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r2.claim: Al-Hawfi calls it لام كي and كي emphatic; the author objects that كي is not causative here and its operation differs.

SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r3.claim: Alternatively, لام marks an eventual result.

SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r4.claim: The Basran analysis, preferred by the author, assigns شيئا to the nearer علم in the competition between يعلم and علم.

SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:16:70/r5.claim: The Kufan attachment to يعلم is rejected because علم would then need a missing object pronoun: علم إياه شيئا.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r1.claim: God creates people from nothing and then causes them to die; some reach old age, when their bodily constitution weakens, as also described in 30:54.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r2.speaker: علي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r2.claim: Ali is reported to identify the most decrepit age as seventy-five.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r3.claim: At this age strength, memory, and knowledge decline into senility, explaining how one may know nothing after having known.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r4.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet sought refuge from miserliness, laziness, senility, decrepit old age, grave punishment, the Dajjal, and the trials of life and death; Muslim transmits the same report.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r5.speaker: زهير بن أبي سلمى
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p585/r5.claim: Zuhayr's Muallaqa says a person tires of life after eighty years and that one who escapes death's random blows lives on into senility.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r1.claim: Human life passes through infancy and growth, youth, maturity with declining strength, and old age with obvious weakness; some die in strength while others reach decrepitude.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r2.claim: The frailest age returns a person to childlike weakness and can bring loss of knowledge, with no medicine or remedy able to avert it; people should reflect before it arrives.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r3.claim: Removing the preposition before “anything” makes ignorance encompass the entire period after knowledge, continuing until death.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p289/r4.claim: God’s knowledge and power encompass all things: whatever He wills occurs, and His power can prevent what He knows will not occur.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r1.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r1.claim: A Prophetic report says flies live forty days and all are in the Fire except bees.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r10.speaker: سعد بن أبي وقاص
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r10.claim: The Prophet sought refuge from miserliness, cowardice, decrepit age, worldly trials, and punishment in the grave.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r2.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r2.claim: A report through Mujahid says all flies are in the Fire except bees and that killing bees was forbidden; its intermediate authority is uncertain between ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn ʿUmar.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r3.claim: A report from the Prophet similarly says that all flies are in the Fire except bees.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r4.speaker: علي
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r4.claim: Ali says the decrepit age begins at seventy-five.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r5.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r5.claim: Al-Suddi glosses decrepit age in this verse as fear.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r6.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r6.claim: Ikrima says whoever recites the Qur'an is not returned to decrepit age, citing the phrase about knowing nothing after knowledge.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r7.speaker: طاوس
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r7.claim: Tawus says a learned person does not become senile; Abd al-Malik reports that Qur'an reciters are said to retain the soundest minds.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r8.speaker: أنس
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r8.claim: The Prophet sought refuge from miserliness, laziness, decrepit age, grave punishment, the Antichrist's trials, and the trials of life and death.

DURR-FULL:v5p146/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r9.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v5p146/r9.claim: A Prophetic supplication seeks refuge from an unheard prayer, an unhumble heart, useless knowledge, an insatiable soul, hunger, treachery, laziness, old age, miserliness, cowardice, the Antichrist, and grave punishment.

BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r1.claim: God knows lifespan measures and can take a vigorous youth or preserve a worn elder; unequal timing reflects wise divine determination rather than natural necessity.

BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r2.claim: Human life is divided into seven stages: childhood to seven, boyhood to fourteen, youth to thirty-two, then middle age and old age through life’s end.

BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r3.speaker: الإرشاد
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r3.claim: Al-Irshad groups life into growth, stable youth, mild decline in middle age, and severe decline in old age; senility is worst because it mimics childhood and has no cure.

BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r4.claim: The Prophet sought refuge from miserliness, laziness, decrepit age, grave punishment, the Antichrist’s trial, and the trials of life and death.

BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r5.speaker: بعضهم
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r5.claim: Some say decrepitude applies to disbelievers, while a Muslim’s reason grows with age through piety; a hadith says Quran reciters are not returned to decrepit age, as are those who reflect and act on it.

BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r6.claim: The claim that scholars escape dementia applies to scholars of the afterlife and those who know God, not all scholars; the author has seen contemporaries regress to childishness.

BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p42#3/r7.claim: Though decrepit age is hard, it is also a time for forgiveness and higher rank; a report says good deeds are confirmed at eighty and sins erased.

BURSEVI:v5p42/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p42/r4.claim: God takes people at different ages, and neither young nor old can advance or delay the appointed term.

BURSEVI:v5p42/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p42/r5.claim: Some are returned to the most decrepit age, where old age and senility weaken body, reason, and understanding; there is no fixed threshold.

BURSEVI:v5p42/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p42/r6.speaker: قتادة
BURSEVI:v5p42/r6.claim: Qatada says reaching ninety can end one’s ability to work, manage affairs, earn, perform pilgrimage, or campaign.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r1.claim: After describing water, plants, livestock, and bees, the passage turns to the stages of human life from birth to death.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r10.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r10.claim: Other readings are that the elderly person learns nothing new, or loses the ability to reason; al-Alusi prefers extreme forgetfulness, with العلم meaning recognition in the main reading.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r11.claim: شيئا may be a cognate accusative or direct object; the syntax may involve shared governance between يعلم and علم, with an omitted object understood generally.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r12.claim: God knows everything, including the wisdom behind creation, death, and return to senility, and has power over all things.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r2.claim: God creates people and takes them at different terms according to wise decree; the phrase about some being returned to senility is evidence for an omitted clause about those who die earlier.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r3.claim: Arذل العمر is the lowest, most feeble period of senility, when strength and senses fail and the person resembles a child; the phrasing figuratively depicts reversal, as in 36:68.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r4.speaker: علي
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r4.claim: Ali is reported to define the oldest age as seventy-five years; Qatada says ninety and another view says ninety-five, while most define it by senility because it varies by constitution.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r5.claim: The phrase applies to believers and unbelievers alike; the claim that only unbelievers reach senility, or that Quran reciters are protected from it, is refuted by observation.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r6.speaker: عكرمة
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r6.claim: Ikrima says whoever recites the Quran will not be returned to the oldest age; al-Alusi rejects the claim as contradicted by experience.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r7.speaker: أنس عن النبي
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r7.claim: The Prophet sought refuge from miserliness, laziness, decrepit old age, grave punishment, the Dajjal's trials, and the trials of life and death.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r8.claim: The lām in لكي signals outcome, though originally it marks purpose; the clause means that a person becomes so forgetful that newly learned information soon vanishes.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r9.speaker: الحوفي
ALUSI-FULL:v14p187#2/r9.claim: Al-Hawfi calls the lām a purpose marker reinforced by كي; al-Alusi rejects this analysis.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r1.claim: God knows the appointed lifespans and can kill a vigorous young person while leaving a decrepit elder alive, showing that lifespan differences reflect wise divine determination rather than nature alone.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r2.claim: Another explanation contrasts human decline in knowledge and power during old age with God's complete knowledge and power, which remain unchanged over time.

ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v14p188/r3.claim: The nominal sentence indicates continued permanence; the attributes are ordered with knowledge first because loss of knowledge has just been mentioned, though their relation to things also explains the ordering.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r1.claim: The argument shifts from fine details in creation to God's irresistible control over people through creation, death, and senility, demonstrating sole lordship and power; the ending names Him knowing and powerful.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r2.claim: Repeating the divine name at the start, as in Q 16:65, makes the subject of the argument explicit; the verbal predicate implies that God alone performs these acts.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r3.claim: Creation is a blessing; death relieves the deceased from senility and renews the generations, though God apportions such benefits as He wills.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r4.claim: The contrast between ordinary death and being returned to extreme old age shows death occurs at its customary time, since reaching senility is uncommon.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r5.claim: أرذل is the superlative of lowliness or poor quality; العمر is a lifetime, from the idea of inhabiting or occupying a place, as in Q 30:9.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p211#2/r6.claim: Calling the lifetime itself “most decrepit” is a rational metaphor: the true referent is the person's aged physical and mental state, not the duration of life.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r1.claim: Senility has no fixed age because it varies with bodies, countries, health, and constitution; it is physical, can affect believers and unbelievers, and the Prophet sought refuge from it.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r2.claim: The lām before كي expresses outcome rather than true purpose, reproaching people's wish for long life: senility makes learning slow, comprehension weak, and forgetting quick, a humiliating decline toward animal-like incapacity.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r3.claim: Using a causal preposition for consequence is a rhetorical form of rebuke or correction, as in Q 3:178 and Q 16:55.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r4.claim: The indefinite علم denotes the whole class of knowledge: the person loses the capacity to learn anything after once knowing.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r5.claim: The ending summarizes God's knowledge and power; knowledge comes first because power acts according to knowledge, and the breadth of knowledge determines the reach of power.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r6.speaker: أبو الطيب
IBNASHUR-FULL:v14p212/r6.claim: Abū al-Ṭayyib's verse illustrates that great ambitions can exhaust the body pursuing what the self desires.

TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r1.claim: Differences among created things make power seem easier or harder according to causes and conditions, but God’s power is identical with His necessary essence and cannot depend on any external condition or absence of impediment.

TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r2.claim: God’s power is unlimited and relates equally to every thing; all existents depend on Him, and creating one thing with all its relations amounts to creating the whole world by one power, with no coequal cause outside it.

TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:65-77#2/r3.claim: This account makes resurrection the reappearance of what was hidden, affirms equal divine power over all things, and shows that things are ultimately interconnected under one power; an ordinary causal view also allows God to act through intermediate causes.

TABATABAI:16:65-77#3/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:65-77#3/r1.speaker: علي عليه السلام
TABATABAI:16:65-77#3/r1.claim: A report from Ali says the worst age is seventy-five; a report from Anas quoting the Prophet gives one hundred, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the reports do not conflict with his explanation.

TABATABAI:16:69-70/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:69-70/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:69-70/r6.claim: The worst stage of life is senility, when perception and memory decline; its onset varies by temperament and usually begins around age seventy-five.

TABATABAI:16:69-70/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:16:69-70/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:16:69-70/r7.claim: People are created, die at ordinary ages, and some return to senility and forget what they knew; this shows people do not control their life, death, or knowledge, which depend on God’s knowledge and power.

ASAD-NOTES:16:70#n79/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:16:70#n79/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:16:70#n79/r1.claim: The verse evokes human growth in strength, intelligence, and experience followed by decay and sometimes senility as helpless as infancy.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:70/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:70/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:70/r1.claim: God creates, sustains, and causes death; idols and false gods do none of these.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:70/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:70/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:16:70/r2.claim: Erzel-i umrun is old age at the weakest, least productive point in bodily and mental capacity; dying may be better than reaching that state, but only God knows what is good and the believer submits to His decree.

STUDYQURAN:16:70/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r1.claim: Life moves from infant weakness to adult strength and then weakness in old age; strength and weakness correspond to degrees of knowledge.

STUDYQURAN:16:70/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r2.claim: Infants know nothing (16:78), while some elderly lose knowledge; unlike human capacities, God's knowledge and power do not wax or wane.

STUDYQURAN:16:70/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r3.claim: God's taking a person unto Himself refers to each individual's earthly death.

STUDYQURAN:16:70/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r4.speaker: Some
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r4.claim: Some identify the weakest age as seventy-five or ninety, when weakness often begins in body and mind.

STUDYQURAN:16:70/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r5.claim: Knowing nothing after knowledge describes forgetfulness and senility affecting some people in advanced age.

STUDYQURAN:16:70/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:16:70/r6.claim: This description does not deny old age's traditional association with wisdom and maturity; shaykh or pīr can denote a Sufi master or learned authority.
